title: An AI Agent Injected Drugs Into a Live Mouse’s Brain
gist: Exin Therapeutics CEO Gabriel Ocana Santero connected an AI agent to a custom robotic rig, and it carried out a gene-therapy brain injection on a live epileptic mouse after a vet surgeon performed the craniotomy. Claude Opus 5.5 refused to do the injection and Claude Sonnet 5 went ahead. A coordinate glitch the agent was not allowed to fix stretched the roughly 45-minute procedure past an hour.

insights.claim: Exin Therapeutics connected an AI agent to a custom surgical rig with a motorized mouse immobilizer, a camera, a robotic needle and controlled compound delivery. The agent picked a gene therapy from 19 spreadsheet options, chose the brain region and coordinates, and controlled injection volume and speed.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Agentic AI is moving from designing experiments to physically running them, which opens a market for lab automation built around agents.
insights.quote: The agent selected the therapy, brain region, and injection coordinates, then controlled the robotic arms and injector needle, as well as all the parameters, such as volume and speed.

themes.theme: Model refusal behavior differs across Claude tiers

insights.claim: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 did the experimental planning but refused to guide the needle into the mouse's brain, warning it might stop midway and endanger the animal. The team switched to Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Safety behavior varies between models from the same lab, so physical-world deployments may route around refusals by switching models.

themes.theme: Safeguards and failure modes in physical agents

insights.claim: The safeguards were human approval of the agent's proposed injection plan, an emergency button that cut power to the rig's motors, and no agent access to the equipment code so it could not change its own operating rules.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: This is a practical template for gating agents that control hardware: plan approval, a kill switch and read-only control code.
insights.quote: They also restricted the agent's access to the underlying equipment code to prevent it from modifying its own operating rules.

insights.claim: A glitch broke the rig's coordinate system. The agent correctly saw that the injection position was wrong but would not fix the code because its instructions forbade it. A second agent running Opus 5, which was not told a live surgery was in progress, made the fix, and the procedure ran slightly over an hour instead of the usual roughly 45 minutes.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Hard restrictions on an agent can conflict with recovering from errors, and teams may get around them by giving information to another agent, which is a governance gap.

insights.claim: Exin plans to test Grok and other models to compare performance. It is also experimenting with craniotomies controlled by an agent but wants to be sure they are safe before trying them in live surgery.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Model vendors will be compared on how they perform in physical lab tasks, not just on benchmarks.
